title: The Supply Side of Social Media
abstract: We study social media’s distinctive model of content production. Unlike legacy media outlets, social media platforms do not professionally produce content designed ex-ante to engage viewers; instead, they harvest content created for nonpecuniary reasons by large numbers of amateur users. The resulting scale and diversity of platforms’ content libraries, combined with their ability to test content on subsets of users, facilitates granular ex-post discovery of pieces that engage each viewer. We develop a model of this process and show that it leads the content consumed in equilibrium to depend on viewer preferences (demand) but also on creator preferences (supply), because the production scale powering platforms’ discovery concentrates where creators are eager to produce. Collecting new data on Instagram, TikTok, and X/Twitter, we show that viewers’ feeds are dominated by amateur creators who produce envy-provoking “lifestyle” and partisan political content in pursuit of social status and expressive satisfaction. To disentangle supply and demand, we experimentally generate shifters on both sides of the market by manipulating viewers’ feeds and eliciting creators’ incentivized preferences while paying them to produce content. On the demand side, pieces of lifestyle and partisan content are less likely to highly engage viewers than more benign entertainment. But these content types enjoy enormous supply-driven production scale. This enables platforms to cherry-pick the minority of such pieces viewers find more engaging than the marginal piece of entertainment. Estimating our model using the experimental variation, we calculate that supply-side preferences account for one- to two-thirds of the prevalence of envy-provoking and partisan content in viewers’ feeds.
